title: Forward: Power Sums ∈ ℚ⟪Elementary Symmetrics⟫
content: psum_mem_adjoin_esymm shows every power sum pₖ lies in the ℚ-subalgebra generated by the elementary symmetric polynomials. The proof is a strong induction (Nat.strongRecOn) using Mathlib's psum_eq_mul_esymm_sub_sum, which writes pₖ via the eᵢ and STRICTLY LOWER power sums pⱼ (j < k). Each piece is placed in the subalgebra by the closure lemmas (mul_mem, sum_mem, pow_mem, natCast_mem); the antidiagonal bound a.2 < k feeds the induction hypothesis. This direction is DIVISION-FREE, so it holds without inverting any integer.
mathContext: $p_k \in \mathbb{Q}\langle e_0, e_1, \ldots\rangle$ for all $k$, via $p_k = e_1 p_{k-1} - \cdots$ (Newton's recurrence, no division).

title: Inverted: Elementary Symmetrics ∈ ℚ⟪Power Sums⟫ (Dual Newton–Girard)
content: esymm_mem_adjoin_psum is the open question's answer: each eₖ lies in the ℚ-subalgebra generated by the power sums. The forward Newton recurrence mul_esymm_eq_sum gives k·eₖ as a combination of lower eᵢ and pⱼ; over a ℚ-algebra k is invertible, so dividing by k expresses eₖ itself recursively. Strong induction then closes it. This inversion is the dual Newton–Girard formula and is exactly where the ℚ-algebra hypothesis is essential.

title: Why a ℚ-Algebra: Inverting k
content: The crux of the inversion: hcancel proves algebraMap ℚ (...) (k⁻¹) · (k : MvPolynomial) = 1 by pushing k⁻¹·k = 1 through the algebra map (map_natCast, map_mul, inv_mul_cancel₀, map_one). This makes the integer k a unit so the recurrence k·eₖ = ... can be solved for eₖ. Over a general commutative ring this step fails — which is why only the explicit low-degree formulae (cleared of denominators) survive there.

title: Newton's Theorem: the Two Subalgebras Coincide
content: adjoin_psum_eq_adjoin_esymm packages both directions into the equality of ℚ-subalgebras Algebra.adjoin ℚ (range psum) = Algebra.adjoin ℚ (range esymm), by le_antisymm: Algebra.adjoin_le_iff reduces each inclusion to membership of the generators, supplied by the two theorems above. This is the multiplicative form of Newton's theorem on symmetric functions — over a ℚ-algebra the power sums and the elementary symmetric polynomials generate the same algebra, hence carry the same symmetric-function information.

title: First Dual Formula e₁ = p₁
content: The degree-1 case is an equality, not just a membership: both e₁ and p₁ equal ∑ᵢ Xᵢ (esymm_one, psum_one), so esymm_one_eq_psum holds over ANY commutative ring with no division. It is the base of the dual recursion and the simplest dual Newton–Girard identity.

title: Second Dual Formula 2·e₂ = p₁² − p₂
content: two_mul_esymm_two records the classical low-degree dual formula in denominator-cleared form, valid over any commutative ring (over a ℚ-algebra it reads e₂ = (p₁² − p₂)/2). The proof specializes mul_esymm_eq_sum at k = 2, evaluates the antidiagonal filter {(0,2),(1,1)} by `decide`, substitutes e₀ = 1 and e₁ = p₁, and closes with linear_combination. It shows the dual formulae have integer-coefficient forms even where the full inversion needs ℚ.
mathContext: $2e_2 = p_1^2 - p_2$ over any commutative ring; $e_2 = \tfrac{p_1^2 - p_2}{2}$ over a ℚ-algebra.
